rd-school-c8-science-a.ch07-adolescence-.title: Reaching the Age of Adolescence — Part 2: The Full Chapter, Section by Section
rd-school-c8-science-a.ch07-adolescence-.subtitle: Puberty changes, secondary sexual characters, hormones, sex determination, endocrine glands, nutrition, hygiene and saying no to drugs

sections.md:
Growth begins at birth, but between about **11 and 19 years** the body changes in special ways. This period of life is **adolescence** — also called **teenage** (thirteen to nineteen). In girls it may begin a year or two earlier than in boys, and its timing varies from person to person.

The body undergoes changes that mark the onset of **puberty**. The most important change is that boys and girls become capable of reproduction. Puberty ends when an adolescent reaches **reproductive maturity**. Everybody's rate of growth is different — there is no 'correct' timing.

**1. Increase in height.** The long bones of the arms and legs elongate, making a person tall. Initially girls grow faster than boys, but by about 18 both reach their maximum height. A rough rule from the chapter: if a boy is 120 cm at 9 years and has reached 75% of his full height, his full height = 120 × 100/75 = **160 cm**.

**2. Change in body shape.** Boys' shoulders broaden and chests widen; muscles grow more prominently. In girls the region below the waist becomes wider.

**3. Voice change.** The **voice box (larynx)** begins to grow. In boys it grows larger and becomes visible as a protruding part of the throat called the **Adam's apple**; the voice becomes hoarse and deeper. In girls the larynx is smaller and hardly visible; their voices are high-pitched. Sometimes a boy's voice 'cracks' while the muscles of the voice box grow.

**4. Increased activity of sweat and sebaceous glands.** This can cause **acne and pimples** on the face — wash your face regularly; don't squeeze pimples.

**5. Development of sex organs.** At puberty, male sex organs like the testes and penis develop completely; testes begin to produce sperms. In girls the ovaries enlarge and eggs begin to mature and be released.

**6. Reaching mental, intellectual and emotional maturity.** Adolescents become more independent and self-conscious, their thinking expands, and they may feel unsure or moody at times — this is normal.

check.q: A girl is 140 cm tall at 10 years and has reached 84% of her full height. Her full height will be about…
check.why: Full height = 140 × 100 ÷ 84 ≈ 166.7 cm.

sections.md:
Features that help to distinguish the male from the female, apart from the reproductive organs, are **secondary sexual characters**: in girls, breasts begin to develop; in boys, hair grows on the face (moustache and beard). Both develop hair under the arms and in the pubic region.

These changes are controlled by **hormones** — chemical substances secreted by **endocrine glands** (ductless glands) directly into the **bloodstream**, which carries them to a target site.

- **Testes** release the male hormone **testosterone** at puberty.
- **Ovaries** produce the female hormone **estrogen**, which makes breasts develop and mammary glands form inside.
- The production of these hormones is under the control of another hormone from the **pituitary gland**.

check.q: Hormones are carried to their target sites by…
check.why: Endocrine glands are ductless and pour hormones directly into the blood, which carries them.

sections.md:
Adolescents become capable of reproduction when testes and ovaries begin producing gametes. The reproductive phase lasts much longer in males. In women it begins at puberty (10–12 years) and generally lasts till about **45–50 years**.

The ovum matures and is released by one ovary once in about **28–30 days**. Each month the wall of the uterus thickens to receive a fertilised egg. If fertilisation does not occur, the egg and the thickened lining with its blood vessels are shed — this is **menstruation**, which occurs once in about 28–30 days.

The first menstrual flow at puberty is **menarche**; its stopping at 45–50 years is **menopause**. Cycles may be irregular initially — if worries persist, a doctor should be consulted. The cycle is controlled by hormones.

check.q: The first menstrual flow is called…
check.why: Menarche is the first menstruation at puberty; menopause is when it stops.

sections.h: How is the sex of the baby determined?
sections.md:
Inside the fertilised egg are the instructions that decide the sex. All human beings have **23 pairs of chromosomes** in the nucleus of their cells. Two of these are **sex chromosomes**, named **X and Y**.

- A female has **two X** chromosomes.
- A male has **one X and one Y**.

All eggs carry an X. Sperms are of two kinds: half carry X, half carry Y.

- X sperm + egg → **XX → girl**.
- Y sperm + egg → **XY → boy**.

So the **sex of the child is determined by the father's sperm**, not the mother. Blaming a mother for the sex of a child is scientifically wrong and unfair.

| Egg | Sperm | Zygote | Child |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | X | XX | Girl |
| X | Y | XY | Boy |

fig.caption: Every egg carries X; the sperm carries X or Y, so the sperm decides the baby's sex.
fig.alt: Two eggs labelled X meeting sperms labelled X and Y, giving XX girl and XY boy

check.q: A zygote with XY chromosomes develops into…
check.why: XY means a Y-carrying sperm fertilised the egg, so the child is a boy.

sections.md:
| Gland | Hormone / role |
|---|---|
| **Pituitary** (in the brain) | Growth hormone and hormones that control other glands — called the master gland |
| **Thyroid** (in the neck) | **Thyroxine**; lack of iodine in diet can cause **goitre** (swollen neck) |
| **Pancreas** | **Insulin**; too little causes **diabetes** |
| **Adrenals** (on the kidneys) | **Adrenalin** — helps cope with stress, anger, worry; also keeps salt level in blood correct |
| Testes / Ovaries | Testosterone / estrogen and progesterone |

If the growth hormone from the pituitary is not produced in the right quantity, a person may grow too tall or remain very short.

**Hormones in insects and frogs.** **Metamorphosis** — from caterpillar to moth, tadpole to frog — is controlled by insect hormones and, in frogs, by **thyroxine** from the thyroid; thyroxine production needs **iodine** in water. If pond water lacks iodine, tadpoles cannot become adults.

check.q: Which hormone deficiency is linked with diabetes?
check.why: Insulin from the pancreas controls blood sugar; too little insulin causes diabetes.

sections.h: Reproductive health: food, hygiene, exercise and saying no to drugs
sections.md:
**Nutritional needs.** Adolescence is a period of rapid growth, so a **balanced diet** is vital: proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins and minerals in the right proportion. Indian meals like roti/rice, dal and vegetables form a balanced diet. Milk is a balanced food in itself. **Iron** (leafy vegetables, jaggery, meat, citrus, amla) builds blood; **iodine** (iodised salt) for the thyroid. Avoid relying on chips and packaged snacks.

**Personal hygiene.** Bathe at least once a day, especially in hot weather when sweat glands are active; clean all body parts and wear clean clothes. Girls should keep track of the cycle and use clean sanitary napkins or pads, changing them every 4–5 hours as needed.

**Physical exercise.** Walking, playing outdoors and sport keep the body fit and the mind fresh.

**Say 'NO' to drugs.** Curiosity and peer pressure may tempt some adolescents. Drugs are **addictive**, harm health and happiness, and you may not be able to stop once you start. Avoid them. Also know that **HIV/AIDS** can spread from an infected person through sharing syringes, from an infected mother to the baby, or through sexual contact — so never share needles.

**Myths and facts.** A girl becomes pregnant if she looks at boys during menstruation — **false**. The mother is responsible for the sex of the child — **false**. A girl should not be allowed to work in the kitchen during menstruation — **false**; this is a myth.

**Adolescent pregnancy.** In India, the legal age of marriage is **18 for girls and 21 for boys**. Early marriage and motherhood cause health problems for mother and child and cut short education and employment.

check.q: Which nutrient from iodised salt prevents goitre?
check.why: Iodine is needed to make thyroxine; its lack causes the thyroid to swell, called goitre.

summary: Adolescence (about 11–19 years) is when the body changes towards reproductive maturity; puberty marks its onset.
Changes: height, body shape, voice, sweat and sebaceous glands, sex organs, and emotional maturity.
Adam's apple is the enlarged larynx in boys.
Secondary sexual characters include beard in boys and breasts in girls.
Testosterone (testes) and estrogen (ovaries) are controlled by pituitary hormones.
Menstruation occurs every 28–30 days; menarche begins it, menopause ends it.
Females are XX, males XY; the father's sperm determines the child's sex.
Endocrine glands: pituitary, thyroid, pancreas, adrenals, testes, ovaries.
Lack of iodine causes goitre; lack of insulin causes diabetes.
Thyroxine (needs iodine) controls metamorphosis in tadpoles.
Balanced diet, hygiene, exercise and avoiding drugs keep adolescents healthy.
Legal age of marriage in India: 18 for girls, 21 for boys.

rd-school-c8-science-b.ch08-force-pressu.title: Force and Pressure
rd-school-c8-science-b.ch08-force-pressu.subtitle: Pushes, pulls, sharp knives, camel feet and the invisible weight of the air on your head

sections.h: Every action is a push or a pull
sections.md:
Watch a cricket match for a minute. The bowler swings his arm and the ball leaves his hand. The batter swings and the ball reverses direction. A fielder dives and stops it dead. The ball speeds up, changes direction, stops — and every change is caused by something pushing or pulling it.

In science, **a push or a pull on an object is called a force**. Opening a door, kicking a football, lifting a school bag, pulling a bucket from a well, squeezing toothpaste — all involve force.

**Forces are due to an interaction.** At least **two objects must interact** for a force to come into play. A man pushing a stationary car is applying a force; if he stops touching it, there's no force from him. In a tug-of-war, two teams pull a rope in opposite directions.

**Exploring forces:**
- Forces applied on an object **in the same direction add** to one another.
- If two forces act in **opposite directions**, the net force is the **difference** between the two, and the object moves in the direction of the larger force.
- If equal forces act in opposite directions, the net force is zero and nothing moves — like an evenly matched tug-of-war.

The strength of a force is expressed by its **magnitude**. Force also has a **direction**. If either changes, its effect changes. The SI unit of force is the **newton (N)**.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#f3fbff'/><rect y='200' width='600' height='60' fill='#9ccc65'/><g><line x1='80' y1='150' x2='520' y2='150' stroke='#8d6e63' stroke-width='6'/><rect x='296' y='140' width='8' height='22' fill='#e53935'/><g fill='#1e88e5'><circle cx='90' cy='120' r='14'/><rect x='80' y='134' width='20' height='50' rx='6'/><circle cx='140' cy='120' r='14'/><rect x='130' y='134' width='20' height='50' rx='6'/></g><g fill='#fb8c00'><circle cx='460' cy='120' r='14'/><rect x='450' y='134' width='20' height='50' rx='6'/><circle cx='510' cy='120' r='14'/><rect x='500' y='134' width='20' height='50' rx='6'/></g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;-30 0;-10 0;-45 0;0 0' dur='5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><line x1='300' y1='60' x2='300' y2='210' stroke='#555' stroke-dasharray='5 5'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='15'><text x='60' y='40' fill='#1565c0'>← 500 N</text><text x='470' y='40' fill='#ef6c00'>400 N →</text><text x='200' y='240' fill='#fff'>Net force = 100 N towards the left</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Tug-of-war: opposite forces subtract. The rope moves towards the stronger team.
fig.alt: Two teams pulling a rope, the rope sliding left towards the stronger team

keyTerms: Force — push or pull
Net force — combined effect of all forces on an object
Newton (N) — SI unit of force

check.q: Two boys push a box: one with 30 N to the right, the other with 50 N to the left. The net force is…
check.why: Opposite forces subtract: 50 − 30 = 20 N, acting in the direction of the larger force, to the left.

sections.md:
A force can produce several effects:

1. **Change the state of motion.** It can make a stationary object move (a football kicked), stop a moving object (goalkeeper catching it), or change its speed (pedalling harder). The **state of motion** of an object is described by its **speed and direction**. The state of rest is considered to be a state of zero speed.
2. **Change the direction of motion** — a batter deflecting a ball.
3. **Change the shape of an object** — pressing a ball of dough into a roti, squeezing a sponge, stretching a rubber band, pressing a balloon.

All these effects may happen together. Note: a force may not always change the state of motion — pushing a wall hard does not move it. But a change in the state of motion or shape **always** requires a force.

> Did you know? When you roll a ball on a flat floor, it slows down and stops by itself. Something must be pushing it back — that's friction, the subject of the next chapter.

**Muscular force:** the force resulting from the action of muscles. We use it to walk, lift, push and chew. Animals like bullocks, horses, donkeys and camels use muscular force to carry out tasks for us. Since it can be applied only when it is in contact with an object, it is a **contact force**.

**Friction:** a ball rolling on the ground gradually slows. A boat stops when you stop rowing. The force responsible is **friction** — it always **acts on all moving objects** and its direction is always **opposite** to the direction of motion. It arises from contact between surfaces, so it is also a contact force.

check.q: Friction acts…
options: Opposite to the direction of motion
check.why: Friction always opposes motion, which is why a rolling ball slows down and stops.

sections.md:
Some forces act **without touching**.

**Magnetic force:** bring a magnet near another magnet's pole — like poles repel, unlike poles attract. A magnet attracts iron pins from a distance. The force exerted by a magnet is a non-contact force.

**Electrostatic force:** rub a plastic straw with paper and bring it near small bits of paper — they jump to it. The straw has acquired an **electric charge**. The force exerted by a charged body on another charged or uncharged body is an **electrostatic force**. It also acts at a distance.

**Gravitational force:** a coin dropped from your hand falls to the ground; water flows downhill. Objects fall because **the Earth pulls them towards itself**. This is **gravity**. Gravity is a property of **all objects** in the universe — every object pulls every other object — though only very large bodies like Earth produce a strong effect. Gravity keeps the Moon going around the Earth and the Earth around the Sun.

check.q: Which of these is a non-contact force?
check.why: Gravity pulls objects towards the Earth without touching them, so it acts at a distance.

sections.h: Pressure: why a knife is sharp
sections.md:
Why does a porter put a round cloth on his head before lifting a heavy box? Why are school bag straps wide? Why is it easier to push a nail in with its pointed end than with its head? The answer is **pressure**.

**Pressure is force acting on a unit area of a surface.**

> **Pressure = Force ÷ Area on which it acts**

The SI unit of pressure is **newton per square metre (N/m²)**, also called the **pascal (Pa)**.

For the **same force**, a **smaller area** means **greater pressure**, and a **larger area** means **smaller pressure**.

- A **sharp knife** has a very thin edge (tiny area), so pressing gives huge pressure and it cuts easily. A blunt knife spreads the force over more area.
- **Nails and pins** have pointed tips.
- **Shoulder bags** have wide straps to reduce pressure on your shoulder.
- A **porter's cloth turban** increases the area of contact, reducing pressure on his head.
- **Camels** have wide, flat feet so they don't sink into sand; **tractors and tanks** have broad tyres or tracks.
- **Railway tracks** rest on wide sleepers that spread the train's weight.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fffdf5'/><rect y='220' width='600' height='80' fill='#ffe0b2'/><g><polygon points='140,90 160,90 152,215 148,215' fill='#78909c'/><rect x='120' y='70' width='60' height='20' fill='#546e7a'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 -30;0 20;0 20;0 -30' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><g><rect x='390' y='80' width='120' height='30' fill='#90a4ae'/><rect x='420' y='60' width='60' height='20' fill='#546e7a'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;0 108;0 108;0 0' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='15' fill='#333'><text x='70' y='40'>Same force, tiny area</text><text x='70' y='60' fill='#c62828'>HIGH pressure → sinks in</text><text x='360' y='40'>Same force, large area</text><text x='360' y='60' fill='#2e7d32'>LOW pressure → stays on top</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: The same push on a pointed pin goes deep; spread over a flat block, it barely dents the surface.
fig.alt: A pin driven into soft ground versus a wide block resting on it

check.q: Why do school bags have broad straps?
options: To increase pressure on the shoulder
To spread the weight over a larger area and reduce pressure
check.why: A wider strap increases the area of contact, so the same weight produces less pressure on the shoulder.

sections.md:
**Liquids exert pressure on the walls of their container.** Take a plastic bottle and make holes at different heights. Fill it with water: water spurts out of all holes, showing pressure on the walls. The jet from the **lowest hole travels farthest** — liquid pressure **increases with depth**.

That's why **dams are made thicker at the bottom** than at the top, and why a diver deep underwater feels pressure in the ears.

Make holes at the same height around a bottle: water spurts equally in all directions. **A liquid exerts equal pressure at the same depth.**

**Gases exert pressure too.** A balloon or a bicycle tube stays inflated because the air inside presses on its walls. If there's a puncture, air rushes out. Gas pressure also acts in all directions.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 320' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='320' fill='#eef7ff'/><rect x='150' y='40' width='100' height='250' fill='#bbdefb' stroke='#1565c0' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='150' y='60' width='100' height='230' fill='#42a5f5' opacity='.6'/><g fill='none' stroke='#1e88e5' stroke-width='5' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-dasharray='6 10'><path d='M250 110 Q285 120 300 290'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='16;0' dur='.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><path d='M250 180 Q330 190 380 290'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='16;0' dur='.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><path d='M250 250 Q400 255 470 295'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='16;0' dur='.5s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path></g><rect y='295' width='600' height='25' fill='#8d6e63'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' fill='#0d47a1'><text x='20' y='115'>shallow: weak jet</text><text x='20' y='255'>deep: strongest jet</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Water spurts farther from the lower holes because liquid pressure increases with depth.
fig.alt: Bottle of water with three holes; the lowest jet reaches farthest

check.q: Dams are built thicker at the base because…
options: Water is colder at the bottom
check.why: The deeper the water, the greater the pressure it exerts, so the base of the dam must withstand the most force.

sections.md:
We are surrounded by an envelope of air called the **atmosphere**, extending many kilometres above Earth's surface. The pressure exerted by this air is **atmospheric pressure**.

Take a rubber sucker and press it hard on a smooth flat surface. It sticks! Pressing squeezes out most of the air between the cup and surface. The atmospheric pressure outside presses the sucker against the surface. To pull it off you need a large force — enough to overcome atmospheric pressure.

How big is it? Imagine a 15 cm × 15 cm area on your head. The air above presses with a force roughly equal to the weight of **about 225 kg**! Why aren't we crushed? Because the pressure **inside our bodies** is also equal to atmospheric pressure and **cancels** the pressure from outside.

> Did you know? Otto von Guericke, a German scientist, pumped air out of two joined metal hemispheres in the 1650s. Teams of horses could not pull them apart — atmospheric pressure held them together. This is the famous Magdeburg hemispheres experiment.

workedExamples.q: A box weighing 600 N rests on a face of area 0.5 m². Find the pressure. If it is turned to rest on a face of 0.2 m², what is the new pressure?
workedExamples.answer: 1200 Pa, then 3000 Pa — smaller area, larger pressure.

workedExamples.q: A girl weighing 450 N stands on both feet (total area 0.03 m²). What pressure does she exert? What if she stands on one foot?
steps: One foot: area = 0.015 m², so 450 ÷ 0.015 = 30000 Pa
workedExamples.answer: 15,000 Pa on two feet; 30,000 Pa on one foot (double).

workedExamples.q: A drawing pin has a tip of area 0.000001 m². A thumb pushes it with 20 N. Find the pressure at the tip.
workedExamples.answer: 2 crore pascals — that is why it enters wood so easily.

workedExamples.q: Two forces of 8 N and 5 N act on a trolley in the same direction. A third force of 6 N acts opposite. Find the net force.
workedExamples.answer: 7 N in the direction of the 8 N and 5 N forces.

summary: A force is a push or a pull, arising from an interaction between at least two objects.
Forces in the same direction add; in opposite directions they subtract.
Force has magnitude and direction; SI unit is the newton (N).
A force can change speed, direction of motion and shape of an object.
Contact forces: muscular force, friction.
Non-contact forces: magnetic, electrostatic, gravitational.
Gravity is a property of all objects; Earth's gravity makes things fall.
Pressure = Force ÷ Area; SI unit N/m² or pascal (Pa).
Smaller area → greater pressure (knives, nails); larger area → less pressure (bag straps, camel feet).
Liquids exert pressure on walls; it increases with depth and is equal in all directions at a given depth.
Gases exert pressure in all directions.
Atmospheric pressure is huge but balanced by pressure inside our bodies.

glossary.d: Size or strength of a force
Force exerted by a charged body
Pull of the Earth (and every object) on other objects
SI unit of pressure, 1 N/m²
Pressure exerted by the air around us

Why do camels walk easily in a desert?

Why are tractor tyres made broad?

rd-school-c8-science-b.ch08-force-pressu.title: Force and Pressure — Part 2: The Full Chapter, Section by Section
rd-school-c8-science-b.ch08-force-pressu.subtitle: Push and pull, interactions, effects of force, contact and non-contact forces, pressure, liquids, gases and the atmosphere

sections.h: Force — a push or a pull; forces are due to interaction
sections.md:
Opening a door, kicking a football, lifting a school bag, pulling a drawer — every action is a **push or a pull**. A push or pull on an object is a **force**.

At least **two objects must interact** for a force to come into play. A man pushing a stationary car interacts with the car; if he stops pushing, there is no force. In a **tug-of-war**, both teams pull the rope in opposite directions; if they pull equally hard, the rope doesn't move.

**Exploring forces.** Forces applied in the **same direction add up**; forces in **opposite directions** — the net force is the **difference** of the two, acting in the direction of the larger force. Two friends pushing a heavy box together move it more easily.

The **strength** of a force is its **magnitude**; a force also has a **direction**. If either changes, the effect changes. The SI unit of force is the **newton (N)**.

check.q: Two teams pull a rope with 500 N and 420 N in opposite directions. The net force is…
check.why: Opposite forces subtract: 500 − 420 = 80 N, acting towards the stronger team.

sections.md:
A force can:

1. **Make an object move from rest** — pushing a ball on the ground.
2. **Change the speed** of a moving object — hitting a moving ball harder speeds it up; applying brakes slows a bicycle.
3. **Change the direction** of motion — a batsman hitting a ball towards the boundary; a footballer's header.
4. **Change the shape** of an object — pressing dough into a roti, squeezing a rubber ball, stretching a rubber band, pressing a balloon.

The **state of motion** of an object is described by its speed and direction. Rest is speed zero. A force may change either or both.

A force may not always produce a change: pushing a wall hard doesn't move it.

check.q: Which is an example of force changing the shape of an object?
options: A ball rolling to a stop
check.why: Pressing and rolling dough changes its shape, which is one effect of force.

sections.md:
**Muscular force** — force from the action of our muscles; used in walking, chewing, lifting. Animals like bullocks, horses and camels use muscular force to do work for us. It acts only when there is **contact**, so it is a contact force.

**Friction** — a ball rolling on the ground slows down and stops; a bicycle stops when we stop pedalling. The force due to rubbing between surfaces in contact is **friction**; it always acts opposite to motion. It is a contact force (studied in detail in the next chapter).

**Magnetic force.** Bring one magnet near another: like poles repel, unlike poles attract — even without touching. A magnet attracts iron pins from a distance. Magnetic force is a **non-contact force**.

**Electrostatic force.** Rub a plastic straw with paper and bring it near small bits of paper — they are attracted. A charged body exerts **electrostatic force** on another charged or uncharged body, without contact.

**Force of gravity.** Objects fall towards the earth because the earth pulls them. This attractive force is **gravity** (or gravitation). Water flows downwards because of gravity. Gravity is a property of all objects in the universe — every object pulls every other object, though the pull between small objects is tiny.

| Contact | Non-contact |
|---|---|
| Muscular force | Magnetic force |
| Friction | Electrostatic force |
| | Gravitational force |

check.q: Which of these is a non-contact force?
check.why: A charged straw attracts paper bits without touching them, so electrostatic force acts without contact.

sections.md:
Why are porters' head-loads carried on a round cloth? Why does a sharp knife cut better than a blunt one? The answer is **pressure**.

**Pressure = Force ÷ Area on which it acts.** Force acting perpendicular to a surface is called **thrust**. SI unit of pressure: **N/m² = pascal (Pa)**.

Smaller area → larger pressure for the same force:
- Nails, needles and knives have sharp, pointed edges → large pressure for cutting or piercing.
- School bags have **broad straps**, and porters place a round cloth on the head → force spreads over a large area → less pressure, less pain.
- Wide tyres for heavy vehicles and broad feet of camels stop them sinking.

**Example:** a box weighing 600 N rests on a face of area 0.5 m² → pressure 1,200 Pa; turned onto a face of 0.2 m² → 3,000 Pa.

check.q: Why does a school bag have broad straps?
options: To increase pressure on the shoulders
To spread the weight over a larger area and reduce pressure
check.why: A broad strap increases the area, so the same weight produces less pressure on the shoulders.

sections.h: Pressure exerted by liquids and gases
sections.md:
**Liquids press on the bottom.** Fix a balloon/rubber sheet at the bottom of a pipe and pour water in — the sheet bulges more as the water column gets taller. So liquid pressure **increases with depth (height of the column)**.

**Liquids press on the walls too.** Fix a rubber sheet over a side opening of a bottle and fill water — it bulges. A bottle with holes at the same height in its sides sends out equal streams in all directions: **a liquid exerts equal pressure at the same depth**. A bottle with holes at different heights: water from the **lowest hole** spurts the farthest. That's why **dams have thicker walls at the bottom**, and water tanks are kept high for good flow.

**Gases exert pressure.** A balloon or a cycle tube inflates because air particles hit the walls in all directions. A punctured tyre goes flat because the air escapes.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#eff6ff'/><rect x='150' y='40' width='120' height='240' fill='#bfdbfe' stroke='#1e3a8a' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='150' y='60' width='120' height='220' fill='#60a5fa' opacity='0.7'/><g stroke='#2563eb' stroke-width='4' fill='none' stroke-dasharray='10 8'><path d='M270 110 Q300 115 320 160'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='36;0' dur='0.8s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><path d='M270 180 Q330 185 380 260'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='36;0' dur='0.6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><path d='M270 250 Q380 255 470 290'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='36;0' dur='0.45s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='13' fill='#1e3a8a'><text x='330' y='110'>top hole: short jet</text><text x='400' y='200'>middle hole</text><text x='420' y='250'>bottom hole: farthest</text><text x='60' y='170'>deeper</text><text x='60' y='190'>= more</text><text x='60' y='210'>pressure</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Water from the lowest hole travels farthest because liquid pressure increases with depth.
fig.alt: Water container with three holes; flowing jets get longer from top to bottom

check.q: Why are dam walls thicker at the bottom?
options: Water pressure is greatest at the bottom
Water is lighter at the bottom
check.why: Liquid pressure increases with depth, so the bottom of the wall must withstand the greatest pressure.

sections.md:
The envelope of air around the earth is the **atmosphere**, extending many kilometres up. The pressure exerted by this air is **atmospheric pressure**.

**Sucker activity.** Press a rubber sucker on a smooth surface — it sticks. Pressing pushes out most of the air between the sucker and the surface; atmospheric pressure on the outside holds it there. Pulling it off is hard.

**How big is it?** The force of air on an area of 15 cm × 15 cm is about equal to the weight of **225 kg** — roughly the force of gravity on 225 kg. We are not crushed because the **pressure inside our bodies is also equal to atmospheric pressure** and cancels it.

**Did you know?** In 1654, Otto von Guericke of Germany showed the power of air pressure: he pumped air out of two joined metal hemispheres, and teams of horses could not pull them apart.

More everyday examples: drinking through a straw, filling an ink dropper, and the working of a syringe all rely on atmospheric pressure.

check.q: Why are we not crushed by atmospheric pressure?
options: The pressure inside our bodies equals atmospheric pressure
Atmospheric pressure acts only on buildings
check.why: The pressure inside our body balances the outside air pressure, so there is no net crushing force.

workedExamples.q: A force of 50 N acts on an area of 0.25 m². Find the pressure.
A brick of weight 30 N measures 0.2 m × 0.1 m × 0.05 m. Find the least and greatest pressure it can exert.
Two forces of 8 N and 5 N act on a box in the same direction. Find the net force; then if opposite.
workedExamples.answer: 13 N; 3 N towards the 8 N force

summary: A force is a push or a pull, arising from interaction between at least two objects.
Forces in the same direction add; in opposite directions the net force is the difference.
A force has magnitude and direction; SI unit is the newton (N).
Force can start motion, change speed or direction, or change shape.
Contact forces: muscular force, friction. Non-contact: magnetic, electrostatic, gravitational.
Pressure = force ÷ area; unit pascal (Pa = N/m²).
Small area means large pressure (knives, nails); large area means small pressure (broad straps, wide tyres).
Liquid pressure increases with depth and is equal in all directions at the same depth.
Gases exert pressure on the walls of their container.
Atmospheric pressure is large but balanced by the pressure inside our bodies.

rd-school-c8-science-b.ch09-friction.title: Friction
rd-school-c8-science-b.ch09-friction.subtitle: The force that lets you walk, stops your cycle, wears out your shoes — and lights a matchstick

sections.md:
Picture this: you wake up and friction has vanished. You step out of bed and your feet slide away. You cannot hold a glass — it slips through your fingers. Knots untie themselves, nails pop out of walls, buses cannot stop at bus stops, and once something starts moving it never stops. You cannot even write: the pencil would glide across the paper leaving no mark.

That nightmare tells you how important friction is. Yet friction also wears out shoe soles, tyres and machine parts, and wastes fuel. It is both **friend and foe**.

You already know that a ball rolling on the ground gradually slows down and stops. **Friction** is the force that opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact. It acts on both surfaces.

Push a book gently along a table — it stops. Push it in the opposite direction — it stops again. Friction always opposes the **applied force**, whichever way you push.

check.q: Friction opposes…
options: The relative motion between surfaces in contact
check.why: Friction arises where two surfaces touch and always acts to resist their sliding over each other.

sections.md:
Even surfaces that look smooth have tiny bumps and hollows — **irregularities**. Under a microscope, a polished steel sheet looks like a mountain range.

When two surfaces are in contact, these irregularities **interlock**. To move one surface over the other, we must apply force to overcome this interlocking. On **rough surfaces** there are more irregularities, so friction is greater.

Also, the **harder two surfaces are pressed** together, the more friction there is. Try dragging a box with one book in it, then with five books. The heavier box is harder to pull.

**Try it:** make an inclined plane with a board and some bricks. Roll a pencil cell down it onto (a) a smooth floor, (b) a towel spread on the floor, (c) sand. It travels farthest on the smooth floor and least on sand. The rougher the surface, the greater the friction.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#f7f7fb'/><text x='300' y='30' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='17' fill='#333'>Magnified: tiny bumps interlock</text><g><path d='M100 130 l20 20 l20 -15 l15 25 l25 -20 l20 22 l25 -18 l20 20 l25 -25 l20 22 l25 -15 l20 20 l25 -20 l20 22 l25 -18 l20 20 V80 H100Z' fill='#ffb74d' stroke='#e65100' stroke-width='2'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;30 -6;30 0;0 0' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><path d='M80 175 l20 -20 l20 18 l15 -25 l25 20 l20 -22 l25 18 l20 -20 l25 25 l20 -22 l25 15 l20 -20 l25 20 l20 -22 l25 18 l20 -20 l20 20 V260 H80Z' fill='#90a4ae' stroke='#37474f' stroke-width='2'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14'><text x='420' y='100' fill='#e65100'>block (moving →)</text><text x='420' y='240' fill='#37474f'>floor</text><text x='60' y='290' fill='#c62828'>← friction opposes the motion</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Zoom in on any surface and you find hills and valleys. Interlocking bumps resist sliding.
fig.alt: Two jagged surfaces meeting, the upper one sliding and catching on the lower

keyTerms: Irregularities — tiny bumps on a surface
Interlocking — bumps catching on each other

check.q: Friction is greater on rough surfaces because…
options: They have more irregularities that interlock
check.why: Rough surfaces have more and larger bumps that lock into one another, so more force is needed to slide them.

sections.md:
Try pushing a heavy almirah. At first it refuses to budge. Push harder — suddenly it starts sliding, and keeping it moving feels a little easier.

- **Static friction** comes into play when we try to move an object **at rest**.
- **Sliding friction** comes into play when the object is **sliding**.

**Sliding friction is slightly smaller than static friction.** When an object starts sliding, the contact points on its surface do not get enough time to lock into the contact points on the floor. So it's easier to keep something moving than to start moving it.

You can measure friction with a **spring balance** — a device with a coiled spring that stretches when force is applied, with a pointer on a scale in newtons. Attach a brick to it with a string and pull. The reading just before the brick moves is static friction; the reading while it slides steadily is sliding friction.

**Rolling friction:** when one body rolls over the surface of another, the resistance is called rolling friction. **Rolling reduces friction**. It is always easier to roll than to slide a body. That's why a heavy suitcase with wheels is easy to pull, and why we roll a heavy drum rather than drag it.

So: **static > sliding > rolling**.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#fff'/><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' fill='#333'><text x='20' y='40'>Static (largest)</text><text x='20' y='140'>Sliding</text><text x='20' y='240'>Rolling (smallest)</text></g><g fill='#ef5350'><rect x='160' y='25' width='360' height='22' rx='6'><animate attributeName='width' values='0;360' dur='2s' fill='freeze'/></rect></g><g fill='#ffa726'><rect x='160' y='125' width='300' height='22' rx='6'><animate attributeName='width' values='0;300' dur='2s' fill='freeze'/></rect></g><g fill='#66bb6a'><rect x='160' y='225' width='60' height='22' rx='6'><animate attributeName='width' values='0;60' dur='2s' fill='freeze'/></rect></g><g><circle cx='260' cy='270' r='14' fill='none' stroke='#2e7d32' stroke-width='4'/><line x1='260' y1='256' x2='260' y2='284' stroke='#2e7d32' stroke-width='3'><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='rotate' from='0 260 270' to='360 260 270' dur='1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></line></g></svg>
fig.caption: For the same object and surfaces, static friction is largest and rolling friction is much smaller.
fig.alt: Bar chart: static longest, sliding slightly shorter, rolling very short, with a spinning wheel

check.q: Which arrangement is correct?
check.why: Static friction is the largest, sliding friction is slightly smaller, and rolling friction is the smallest.

sections.md:
**Friction is useful:**
- We can **walk** only because friction between shoes and ground stops our feet slipping. On a wet, oily or icy floor it's hard to walk.
- We can **hold** a glass, a pen or a cricket bat because of friction.
- **Writing** with chalk on a blackboard or pencil on paper works because friction rubs off particles.
- **Brakes** on cycles and cars work by friction.
- A **nail** holds in wood and a **knot** holds because of friction.
- **Lighting a matchstick** uses friction to produce heat.
- Buildings can be constructed because friction keeps bricks and mortar in place.

**Friction is harmful:**
- It **wears out** shoe soles, tyres, ball bearings, stairs and machine parts.
- It **produces heat**. Rub your palms together — they get warm. In machines, this heat wastes energy and can damage parts.
- It **wastes fuel and energy**, because engines must work against it.

That's why friction is called a **necessary evil**.

**Friction produces heat** — a lot. When a meteor enters the Earth's atmosphere at high speed, friction with the air heats it so much that it burns and glows. That's a 'shooting star'.

check.q: Which of these is an advantage of friction?
options: Being able to walk without slipping
check.why: Friction between our shoes and the ground grips our feet, letting us walk without slipping.

sections.md:
Sometimes we want *more* friction:
- **Treads** on shoes and tyres — the grooves give better grip on the road. Tyres of a tractor have very deep treads for muddy fields.
- **Brake pads** in cycles and cars press against wheels to increase friction and stop them.
- **Kabaddi players** rub their hands with soil to get a better grip on opponents.
- **Gymnasts** apply a coarse powder on their hands to improve grip.
- **Sports shoes** have spikes; athletes' spikes give extra grip on tracks.
- We sprinkle **sand** on slippery or icy roads.

When treads on a tyre wear out, the tyre becomes smooth and dangerous, especially on wet roads in the monsoon. It must be replaced.

check.q: Why do kabaddi players rub soil on their hands?
check.why: Rough soil particles on the palms increase friction, helping players hold their opponents firmly.

sections.md:
At other times we want *less* friction:
- **Lubricants** — oil, grease or graphite between moving parts form a thin layer, so the irregularities don't interlock. Oil the hinges of a squeaky door; mechanics use grease in bicycle chains. In some machines oil is not advisable, so an **air cushion** is used.
- **Powder on a carrom board** reduces friction so the coins glide.
- **Wheels** — rolling reduces friction, which is why wheels are called one of humanity's greatest inventions. Luggage has wheels.
- **Ball bearings** — steel balls placed between the hubs and axles of ceiling fans, cycles and car wheels. Sliding is replaced by rolling, greatly reducing friction.
- **Polishing surfaces** — friction can never be entirely eliminated; no surface is perfectly smooth, but polishing helps.

> Did you know? A train on rails has very little rolling friction — that's why one locomotive can pull dozens of loaded coaches.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 300' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='300' fill='#eceff1'/><circle cx='300' cy='150' r='120' fill='#90a4ae' stroke='#37474f' stroke-width='4'/><circle cx='300' cy='150' r='60' fill='#cfd8dc' stroke='#37474f' stroke-width='4'/><g><g fill='#fafafa' stroke='#455a64' stroke-width='2'><circle cx='390' cy='150' r='24'/><circle cx='210' cy='150' r='24'/><circle cx='300' cy='240' r='24'/><circle cx='300' cy='60' r='24'/><circle cx='364' cy='214' r='24'/><circle cx='236' cy='86' r='24'/><circle cx='236' cy='214' r='24'/><circle cx='364' cy='86' r='24'/></g><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='rotate' from='0 300 150' to='360 300 150' dur='6s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><circle cx='300' cy='150' r='20' fill='#37474f'/><text x='300' y='290' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='15' fill='#263238'>Ball bearing: steel balls roll between the inner and outer rings</text></svg>
fig.caption: In a ball bearing, rolling balls replace sliding contact, so the wheel turns with very little friction.
fig.alt: Rotating ring of steel balls between inner and outer rings of a bearing

keyTerms: Lubricant — substance that reduces friction
Ball bearing — steel balls that replace sliding with rolling
Tread — grooves that increase grip

sections.md:
Air and water are **fluids** — they can flow. Fluids also exert friction on objects moving through them. This frictional force is called **drag**.

Fluid friction depends on:
- the **speed** of the object relative to the fluid,
- the **shape** of the object,
- the **nature** of the fluid.

When objects move through fluids, they have to overcome friction, losing energy. So we try to **minimise** it, by giving objects special shapes. Where did scientists get the shapes? From nature! **Birds and fish** have bodies pointed at the front and broad in the middle, tapering at the back — a **streamlined shape**. Boats, ships and aeroplanes are designed this way. India's Vande Bharat trains have pointed noses for the same reason.

Cyclists crouch low and racers wear tight clothes to reduce air drag. Parachutes do the opposite — they have a huge area to *increase* drag and slow the fall.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#e3f2fd'/><g stroke='#64b5f6' stroke-width='2' fill='none' stroke-dasharray='14 10'><path d='M0 80 Q300 40 600 80'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='48;0' dur='1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><path d='M0 130 Q300 130 600 130'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='48;0' dur='1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path><path d='M0 180 Q300 220 600 180'><animate attributeName='stroke-dashoffset' values='48;0' dur='1s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></path></g><path d='M180 130 Q260 85 380 110 Q440 120 470 130 Q440 140 380 150 Q260 175 180 130Z' fill='#ff8a65' stroke='#d84315' stroke-width='3'/><circle cx='220' cy='125' r='5' fill='#212121'/><path d='M470 130 l40 -25 l-10 25 l10 25z' fill='#ff8a65' stroke='#d84315' stroke-width='3'/><text x='300' y='240' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif' font-size='15' fill='#0d47a1'>Streamlined shape: water flows smoothly past</text></svg>
fig.caption: A fish's streamlined body lets water slide past with little drag; ships and planes copy this shape.
fig.alt: Fish shape with flowing streamlines moving around it

check.q: Why are aeroplanes streamlined?
check.why: A streamlined shape lets air flow smoothly around the plane, reducing drag and saving fuel.

workedExamples.q: A spring balance reads 12 N just before a box starts to move and 9 N while it slides steadily. What are static and sliding friction? How much less is sliding friction?
workedExamples.answer: Static 12 N, sliding 9 N; sliding is 3 N (25%) less.

workedExamples.q: A suitcase needs 60 N to drag but only 6 N to roll on wheels. By what factor do the wheels reduce the force?

summary: Friction opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact and acts on both.
It is caused by interlocking of irregularities on surfaces.
Friction depends on the nature of surfaces and how hard they are pressed together.
Static friction > sliding friction > rolling friction.
Friction can be measured with a spring balance.
Friction is useful (walking, holding, writing, brakes, matches) and harmful (wear, heat, energy loss) — a necessary evil.
Friction is increased by treads, brake pads, spikes, soil or powder on hands, sand on roads.
Friction is reduced by lubricants, polishing, powder on carrom boards, wheels and ball bearings.
Friction produces heat.
Fluids exert friction called drag, depending on speed, shape and nature of fluid.
Streamlined shapes copied from birds and fish reduce drag.

glossary.d: Friction when trying to move a body at rest
Friction when a body is sliding
Resistance when one body rolls on another
Friction exerted by fluids
Shape that reduces drag

rd-school-c8-science-b.ch09-friction-2.title: Friction — Part 2: The Full Chapter, Section by Section
rd-school-c8-science-b.ch09-friction-2.subtitle: Causes of friction, static, sliding and rolling friction, a necessary evil, increasing and reducing it, wheels, and fluid friction

sections.md:
Gently push a book on a table — it slides a little and stops. Push it the other way — it stops again. A force opposite to the motion must be acting each time. This force is **friction**.

Friction **always opposes the relative motion** between two surfaces in contact; it acts on both surfaces. If you push the book from left to right, friction acts right to left.

Why do we slip on a wet marble floor, or on a banana peel? Because friction there is very small.

check.q: If a book is pushed towards the east on a table, friction acts towards the…
check.why: Friction always opposes the motion, so it acts opposite to the push, towards the west.

sections.md:
**Activity (inclined plane):** make a slope from a board and bricks; let a pencil cell roll down onto a floor covered with a towel, then a polythene sheet, then sand. It travels least on sand and farthest on smooth polythene.

**Activity (spring balance):** pull a brick across the floor with a spring balance, then the same brick wrapped in polythene — the reading changes.

Conclusions:
- Friction depends on the **nature of the surfaces** — rough surfaces give more friction.
- Friction depends on **how hard the surfaces are pressed together** (heavier load → more friction).

**Why?** Even surfaces that look smooth have **irregularities** — tiny hills and valleys visible under a microscope. These **interlock** when two surfaces touch. To move one over the other, the interlocking must be overcome. Rough surfaces have more irregularities; pressing harder makes them interlock more firmly.

fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 600 260' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect width='600' height='260' fill='#fafaf9'/><path d='M0 170 L40 150 L70 175 L110 145 L150 172 L190 148 L230 176 L270 150 L310 174 L350 146 L390 172 L430 150 L470 175 L510 147 L550 172 L600 150 L600 260 L0 260Z' fill='#a8a29e'/><g><path d='M150 60 L450 60 L450 140 L430 162 L400 138 L360 164 L320 140 L280 166 L240 140 L200 162 L150 140Z' fill='#f59e0b' stroke='#92400e' stroke-width='2'/><animateTransform attributeName='transform' type='translate' values='0 0;12 -4;24 0;12 -4;0 0' dur='3s' repeatCount='indefinite'/></g><g font-family='sans-serif' font-size='14' fill='#1c1917'><text x='300' y='100' text-anchor='middle'>Block</text><text x='300' y='240' text-anchor='middle'>Floor (magnified surface)</text><text x='470' y='50'>push →</text><text x='40' y='50'>← friction</text></g></svg>
fig.caption: Magnified, both surfaces are bumpy; their interlocking is what creates friction.
fig.alt: Jagged block surface sitting on a jagged floor surface, rocking slightly as it is pushed

check.q: Friction arises mainly because…
check.why: Microscopic hills and valleys on the two surfaces lock into each other, resisting sliding.

sections.md:
Try to push a heavy box: at first it doesn't move. **Static friction** acts when we try to move an object at rest. Once it starts moving, it is easier to keep it moving — **sliding friction** acts now, and it is **slightly smaller than static friction**. Why? When sliding, the contact points don't get enough time to lock firmly into each other.

When one body **rolls** over another, the resistance is **rolling friction**. Rolling reduces friction greatly: it is easier to roll than to slide. That's why heavy luggage has wheels, and why the invention of the **wheel** is one of humanity's greatest.

**Order:** static friction > sliding friction > rolling friction.

**Ball bearings.** In ceiling fans, bicycle hubs and machine axles, **ball bearings** placed between the hub and the axle replace sliding with rolling, reducing friction.

check.q: Which is the smallest?
check.why: Rolling friction is far smaller than sliding or static friction, which is why wheels and ball bearings help.

sections.md:
**Friction is useful:**
- We can **walk** because friction stops our feet slipping.
- We can **write** — friction between pencil/pen and paper.
- A nail stays in wood, a knot holds, buildings stand, a matchstick lights by rubbing.
- Vehicles move and **brakes** stop them using friction.
- Without friction, a moving object would never stop.

**Friction is harmful:**
- It **wears out** soles of shoes, tyres, steps of foot over-bridges and machine parts.
- It produces **heat**: rub your palms and they warm up; machines heat up, wasting energy.
- More energy is needed to overcome it.

That is why friction is called a **necessary evil**.

check.q: Which is a harmful effect of friction?
options: Machine parts wear out and heat up
check.why: Friction causes wear and wasteful heating of machine parts, which is its harmful side.

sections.md:
**Increasing friction (when useful):**
- **Treads** on shoe soles and tyres grip the ground; car and tractor tyres have deep treads.
- **Brake pads** in bicycles and cars increase friction to stop.
- **Kabaddi players** rub their hands with soil for a better grip; **gymnasts** apply a coarse powder to their hands.
- Sand on a slippery road.

**Reducing friction (when harmful):**
- **Lubricants** — oil, grease or graphite between moving parts form a thin layer so surfaces don't interlock much. Oil on door hinges stops squeaking.
- **Talcum powder** on a carrom board.
- **Wheels** and **ball bearings** (rolling instead of sliding).
- An **air cushion** between parts where oil can't be used.
- Polishing surfaces smooth.

Friction **can never be fully eliminated** — no surface is perfectly smooth.

check.q: Why do kabaddi players rub their hands with soil?
options: To increase friction and get a better grip
check.why: Soil roughens the palms and increases friction, so players can hold opponents better.

sections.md:
Air and liquids are **fluids**. They also exert friction on objects moving through them, called **fluid friction** or **drag**.

Fluid friction depends on the object's **speed**, its **shape**, and the **nature of the fluid**. To overcome drag, objects moving in fluids must spend energy, so we try to minimise it.

That is why **aeroplanes, boats, ships and racing cars** are given special shapes called **streamlined** shapes — pointed at the front and broader in the middle, tapering at the back. Nature does the same: **birds and fish** have streamlined bodies. Cyclists crouch, and swimmers wear tight caps, to reduce drag.

check.q: Why are aeroplanes given a streamlined shape?
options: To reduce fluid friction (drag) of air
check.why: A streamlined shape lets air flow smoothly past, reducing drag so less energy is needed.

summary: Friction opposes relative motion between surfaces in contact and acts on both.
It depends on the nature of surfaces and how hard they are pressed together.
It is caused by interlocking of irregularities on the surfaces.
Static friction > sliding friction > rolling friction.
Wheels and ball bearings reduce friction by rolling.
Friction is a necessary evil: we need it to walk, write and brake, but it causes wear and heat.
It is increased by treads, brake pads, powder or soil for grip.
It is reduced by lubricants, polishing, wheels, ball bearings and air cushions.
Friction can never be eliminated completely.
Fluid friction (drag) depends on speed, shape and fluid; streamlined shapes reduce it.

rd-school-c8-social-a.geo-ch01-resources.title: Resources
rd-school-c8-social-a.geo-ch01-resources.subtitle: Why is water a resource but a rock on Mars isn't (yet)? Utility, value, people — and how to make things last

sections.md:
Look around your home: a steel tumbler, a ceiling fan, rice in the kitchen, a mobile phone charging, a grandmother's recipe for pickle, sunlight through the window. What do these share? Each is **useful** to someone. That is the heart of this chapter.

> Anything that can be used to satisfy a need is a **resource**.

Water satisfies thirst and grows crops. Electricity runs fans. Vegetables feed us. Some resources have **economic value** — they can be bought and sold: metals, land, petrol. Some do not have economic value but are still valuable: a beautiful landscape, clean air, a lullaby that comforts a child. Something has **utility** (usefulness) and that gives it **value**.

**Time and technology** are two important factors that can change substances into resources. Both are linked to the needs of people. People themselves are the most important resource: it is their ideas, knowledge, inventions and discoveries that lead to the creation of more resources. Every discovery or invention leads to many others. The discovery of fire led to cooking and other processes, while the invention of the wheel ultimately resulted in newer modes of transport. The technology to create hydroelectricity has turned energy in fast-flowing water into an important resource.

> **Did you know?** Bauxite sat in the ground for millions of years as a reddish rock. Only after people learnt to extract aluminium from it (19th century) did it become a valuable resource — now in your pressure cooker and in aircraft.

check.q: Which two factors can change a substance into a resource?
check.why: As needs change over time and technology develops, things that were once useless become useful resources — like flowing water turned into hydroelectricity.

sections.md:
Resources are generally classified into **natural**, **human-made** and **human**.

**1. Natural resources** are drawn from nature and used without much modification: the air we breathe, water in rivers and lakes, soils, minerals. Many are free gifts of nature and can be used directly. Sometimes tools and technology may be needed to use a natural resource in the best possible way.

Natural resources can be classified in different ways:

**(a) By level of development and use:**
- **Actual resources** — their quantity is known and they are being used at present. Example: the rich deposits of coal in the Ruhr region of Germany and petroleum in West Asia; the dark soils of the Deccan plateau in Maharashtra.
- **Potential resources** — their entire quantity may not be known, and they are not being used at present; they could be used in the future. The level of technology is not yet advanced enough to utilise them easily. Example: **uranium** found in Ladakh could be used in the future. High-speed winds were a potential resource two hundred years ago; today they are actual resources — wind farms generate energy (e.g., in the Netherlands, and in India in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat).

**(b) By origin:**
- **Abiotic** — non-living: soils, rocks, minerals.
- **Biotic** — living: plants, animals.

**(c) By stock (renewability):**
- **Renewable** — get renewed or replenished quickly. Some are unlimited and not affected by human activities, like solar and wind energy. Yet careless use of some renewables like water, soil and forest can affect their stock. Water seems unlimited, but shortage and drying up of natural sources is a major problem in many parts of the world today.
- **Non-renewable** — have a limited stock; once exhausted they may take thousands of years to be renewed or replenished. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are examples.

**(d) By distribution:**
- **Ubiquitous** — found everywhere, like the air we breathe.
- **Localised** — found only in certain places, like copper and iron ore.

The distribution of natural resources depends on terrain, climate and altitude. Because these factors differ so much over the earth, resources are **unequally distributed**.

sections.md:
**2. Human-made resources.** Sometimes natural substances become resources only when their original form has been changed. Iron ore was not a resource until people learnt to extract iron from it. People use natural resources to make buildings, bridges, roads, machinery and vehicles — these are **human-made resources**. **Technology** is also a human-made resource.

**3. Human resources.** People can make the best use of nature to create more resources when they have the knowledge, skill and technology to do so. That is why human beings are a special resource. People are **human resources**.

Improving the quality of people's skills so that they are able to create more resources is known as **human resource development**. Education and health help in making people a valuable resource.

Think of India's software engineers in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, nurses serving across the world, farmers using drip irrigation in Maharashtra, and ISRO scientists landing a craft on the Moon. In each case, the land or metal is not what creates value alone — skilled, healthy people do.

> **Did you know?** A country with few minerals can still become prosperous by investing in its people. Japan, with limited natural resources, built a powerful economy largely on education, skills and technology.

Pause a moment and think. What would happen if:
- all oil wells ran dry,
- all forests were cut,
- all soil were washed away?

We would be in deep trouble. Using resources carefully and giving them time to get renewed is called **resource conservation**.

Balancing the need to use resources and also conserve them for the future is called **sustainable development**. There are many ways of conserving resources. Each person can contribute by reducing consumption, recycling and reusing things. Ultimately it makes a difference — it is the same simple idea as switching off a light: small acts multiplied by 140 crore people become enormous.

**The 3 Rs**
- **Reduce** — use less. Turn off taps while brushing; carry a cloth bag.
- **Reuse** — use again. Old jam jars as pen stands, envelopes for notes.
- **Recycle** — process into new things. Paper, glass, aluminium cans.

A quick worked example: suppose a leaking tap drips one drop per second and 20 drops make 1 mL. In a day there are 86,400 seconds, so the tap wastes 86,400 ÷ 20 = **4,320 mL ≈ 4.3 litres** a day — about 1,577 litres a year. Fixing one washer saves enough water to fill around eight large overhead tanks' buckets… or simply, a lot of drinking water.

check.q: What is sustainable development?
options: Using all resources as fast as possible
Balancing the use of resources with conserving them for the future
check.why: Sustainable development means meeting today's needs while carefully conserving resources so future generations can meet theirs.

sections.md:
Some principles of sustainable development:

1. Respect and care for all forms of life.
2. Improve the quality of human life.
3. Conserve the earth's vitality and diversity.
4. Minimise the depletion of natural resources.
5. Change personal attitudes and practices towards the environment.
6. Enable communities to care for their own environment.

**Our duty.** It is the duty of every one of us to conserve resources: by not wasting water and electricity, planting and protecting trees, using public transport or cycling, refusing single-use plastic, and spreading awareness. The future of our planet and its people is linked with our ability to maintain and preserve the life-support system that nature provides.

**An Indian example.** In many villages of Rajasthan and Gujarat, communities have revived old water-harvesting structures — *johads*, step-wells and tanks — capturing monsoon rain so wells stay full in summer. In Uttarakhand, the **Chipko** movement (1970s) saw villagers, many of them women, hug trees to stop felling. These are people acting as caretakers of their own environment, exactly as principle 6 suggests.

> **Think:** Which three things in your own house could be reduced, reused or recycled this week? Make a family chart and watch the numbers.

check.q: Which principle is shown when villagers revive their own tanks and johads?
options: Enable communities to care for their own environment
check.why: When local communities manage and protect their water bodies, they are caring for their own environment — a core principle of sustainable development.

Anything that can be used to satisfy a need is a **resource**. Water, electricity, a rickshaw, vegetables and a textbook all have **utility** (usefulness). Utility or usability is what makes an object or substance a resource.

Some resources have **economic value**, some don't. Metals may have economic value (they can be sold); a beautiful landscape may not have a price, but it has value — it satisfies a need. Some resources gain economic value with time: your grandmother's home remedies have no commercial value today, but if they are patented and sold by a medical firm, they may.

sections.md:
Here's a riddle: why do 90% of the world's people crowd onto only about 30% of the land area? Land covers only about **30% of the earth's surface**, and not all of it is habitable. The uneven distribution of population is mainly due to the varied characteristics of land and climate.

The **rugged topography, steep slopes** of mountains, **low-lying areas** susceptible to waterlogging, **desert** areas and **thick forests** are normally sparsely populated or uninhabited. **Plains and river valleys** offer suitable land for agriculture, so they are densely populated — think of the Ganga plains, the Nile valley or the Yangtze.

**Land use.** Land is used for agriculture, forestry, mining, building houses and roads, and setting up industries. This is called **land use**. It is determined by **physical factors** — topography, soil, climate, minerals and availability of water — and **human factors** — population and technology.

Land can also be classified on the basis of ownership: **private land** and **community land**. Private land is owned by individuals, while community land is owned by the community for common uses like collection of fodder, fruits, nuts or medicinal herbs. These community lands are also called **common property resources**.

People and their demands are ever growing, but land availability is limited. The quality of land also differs. Growing population has led to large-scale destruction of forest and arable land, creating fear of losing this natural resource.

**Conservation of land.** Afforestation, land reclamation, regulated use of chemical pesticides and fertilisers, and checks on overgrazing are some common methods used to conserve land resources. Landslides are a related threat.

sections.md:
**Landslides** are simply defined as the mass movement of rock, debris or earth down a slope. They often take place in conjunction with earthquakes, floods and volcanoes. A prolonged spell of rainfall can cause heavy landslides that may block the flow of rivers for quite some time. Formation of river blockades can cause havoc to settlements downstream on bursting.

In hilly terrain, landslides have been a major and widely spread natural disaster that often strike life and property, occupying a position of major concern. India has seen many such events in the Himalaya and the Western Ghats during the monsoon, damaging roads, homes and crops.

**Mitigation techniques**
- **Hazard mapping** to locate areas prone to landslides, so building settlements there can be avoided.
- **Construction of retention walls** to stop land from slipping.
- **Increase in vegetation cover** to arrest landslides — roots bind soil.
- **Surface drainage control works** to control the movement of landslides along with rainwater and spring flows.

> **Did you know?** A single mature tree's root network can bind several cubic metres of soil — that's why deforested slopes slide far more easily.

sections.h: Soil: the thin skin of life
sections.md:
The thin layer of grainy substance covering the surface of the earth is called **soil**. It is closely linked to land. Landforms determine the type of soil. Soil is made up of **organic matter, minerals and weathered rocks** found on the earth. This happens through the process of **weathering**. The right mix of minerals and organic matter makes the soil fertile.

**Factors of soil formation**
- **Parent rock** — determines colour, texture, chemical properties, mineral content, permeability.
- **Climate** — temperature and rainfall influence the rate of weathering.
- **Relief** — altitude and slope determine accumulation of soil.
- **Flora, fauna and micro-organisms** — affect the rate of humus formation.
- **Time** — determines the thickness of the soil profile.

It can take hundreds of years to form just one centimetre of soil!

**Degradation of soil and conservation measures.** Landslides, erosion and depletion are the major threats to soil as a resource. Both human and natural factors can lead to degradation: deforestation, overgrazing, overuse of chemical fertilisers or pesticides, rain wash, landslides and floods. Some methods of soil conservation:

| Method | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Mulching** | Bare ground between plants is covered with organic matter like straw; helps retain soil moisture |
| **Contour barriers** | Stones, grass, soil used to build barriers along contours; trenches collect water |
| **Rock dam** | Rocks piled up to slow the flow of water; prevents gullies |
| **Terrace farming** | Broad flat steps or terraces on steep slopes so flat surfaces are available to grow crops; reduce surface run-off |
| **Intercropping** | Different crops grown in alternate rows and sown at different times to protect soil from rain wash |
| **Contour ploughing** | Ploughing parallel to the contours of a hill slope to form a natural barrier for water to flow down |
| **Shelter belts** | Rows of trees planted in coastal and dry regions to check wind movement and protect soil cover |

sections.md:
Fresh water is one of the most valuable natural resources. Three-fourths of the earth's surface is covered with water, but only a tiny portion is usable. The ocean water is salty, not fit for human consumption. **Fresh water accounts for only about 2.7%**. Nearly 70% of this occurs as ice sheets and glaciers in Antarctica, Greenland and mountain regions; due to their location they are inaccessible. **Only about 1% of fresh water is available and fit for human use.** It is found as groundwater, surface water in rivers and lakes, and water vapour in the atmosphere.

Fresh water can neither be added nor subtracted from the earth. Its total volume remains constant; its abundance only seems to vary because it is in constant motion, cycling through oceans, air, land and back again, through the **water cycle**.

Water is used for drinking, washing, agriculture, industries, generating electricity through reservoirs of dams. Increasing population, rising demand for food and cash crops, increasing urbanisation and rising standards of living are leading to shortages. Many regions of the world, including parts of India, face water scarcity — a drought-prone area or one where water is badly polluted.

**Problems of water availability.** Shortage may be due to variation in seasonal or annual precipitation, or due to over-exploitation and contamination of water sources.

**Conservation of water resources.** Access to clean and adequate water is a major problem. Steps:
- Even sewage and fertilizer/pesticide run-off pollute water; treat industrial effluents and sewage before release.
- Forest and other vegetation cover slow surface run-off and replenish groundwater.
- **Rainwater harvesting** saves surface run-off.
- Canals used for irrigating fields should be properly lined to minimise losses by water seepage.
- **Sprinklers** effectively irrigate areas by checking seepage and evaporation losses.
- In dry regions with high evaporation, **drip or trickle irrigation** is very useful.

The value of water conservation can be seen everywhere: a borewell that fails in May reminds us that the groundwater table is a bank account; we can't keep withdrawing without deposits from the monsoon.
keyTerms: Rainwater harvesting — collecting rain from rooftops or ground for later use
Drip irrigation — water delivered drop by drop to plant roots
Groundwater — water stored beneath the surface in rocks and soil

check.q: About how much of the earth's fresh water is available and fit for human use?
check.why: Most fresh water is locked in ice, so only about 1% is accessible as groundwater, rivers, lakes and vapour.

sections.md:
Natural vegetation and wildlife exist only in the narrow zone of contact between the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere, which we call the **biosphere**. In the biosphere, living beings are inter-related and interdependent on each other for survival. This life-supporting system is known as the **ecosystem**.

Vegetation and wildlife are valuable resources. Plants provide timber, give shelter to animals, produce oxygen, protect soils so essential for growing crops, act as shelter belts, help in storage of underground water, give us fruits, nuts, latex, turpentine oil, gum and medicinal plants, and paper. Wildlife includes animals, birds, insects and aquatic life forms. They provide milk, meat, hides and wool. Insects like **bees** provide honey, help in pollination and have an important role as decomposers. Birds feed on insects and act as decomposers too. **Vultures** feed on dead livestock and are scavengers — considered vital cleaners of the environment. So, animals big or small all are integral to maintaining balance in the ecosystem.

**Distribution of natural vegetation** mainly depends on **temperature and moisture**:
- **Evergreen forests** — heavy rainfall; huge trees that stay green.
- **Deciduous forests** — moderate rainfall; trees shed leaves in a particular season.
- **Grasslands** — less rainfall; grasses and shrubs.
- **Thorny shrubs** — dry regions with low rainfall; deep roots, thick waxy or thorny leaves to cut moisture loss.
- **Tundra** — cold polar regions; mosses and lichens.

**Conservation of natural vegetation and wildlife.** Forests are our wealth, but deforestation, soil erosion, construction, forest fires, tsunami and landslides are the main threats. Poaching has led to a sharp decline in species such as tigers, lions, elephants, deer, black bucks, crocodiles, rhinoceros, snow leopards, ostriches and peacocks.

Conservation steps: **national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves**; awareness programmes like **social forestry** and **Vanamahotsava** (tree planting); bans on hunting and trade; and **CITES** — the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora — an international agreement that ensures trade in wild animals and plants does not threaten their survival. Roughly 5,000 animal species and 28,000 plant species are protected under it. Bears, dolphins, cacti, corals, orchids and aloes are some examples.

> **Did you know?** India's vulture population crashed by over 95% from the 1990s because cattle were treated with a painkiller, diclofenac, that poisons vultures. Banning its veterinary use was a key conservation step.

sections.md:
Land is among the most important natural resources. It covers only about **30% of the earth's surface**, and not all of it is habitable. Uneven population distribution follows land and climate: rugged mountains, steep slopes, low-lying areas prone to waterlogging, deserts and thick forests are sparsely populated; plains and river valleys are densely populated because they suit agriculture.

**Land use** — using land for agriculture, forestry, mining, roads, industries — is determined by **physical factors** (topography, soil, climate, minerals, water) and **human factors** (population, technology). Land can also be classified by ownership as **private land** and **community land** (used by all for fodder, fruits, nuts, medicinal herbs — also called common property resources).

Growing population means more demand for land; forests are cut and land degrades. **Land degradation**, **landslides**, **soil erosion** and **desertification** are major threats.

**Conservation of land:** afforestation, land reclamation, regulated use of chemical pesticides and fertilisers, and checks on overgrazing.

check.q: Roughly what fraction of the earth's surface is land?
check.why: Land covers only about 30% of the earth's surface, and not all of it is habitable.

sections.md:
**Landslides** are the mass movement of rock, debris or earth down a slope. They often accompany earthquakes, floods and volcanic eruptions; prolonged heavy rain can also cause heavy landslides that block rivers for some time. In hilly areas of India (e.g. the Himalaya and Western Ghats), landslides in the monsoon damage roads, homes and lives.

**Mitigation techniques:**
- **Hazard mapping** to locate landslide-prone areas and avoid building settlements there.
- **Retention walls** to stop land from slipping.
- Increasing **vegetation cover**.
- **Surface drainage control** to control movement of landslides along with rainwater and spring flows.

The thin layer of grainy substance covering the earth's surface is **soil**. It is closely linked to land; landforms determine the type of soil. Soil is made of organic matter, minerals and weathered rocks. The right mix of minerals and organic matter makes soil fertile.

**Weathering** — breaking up and decay of exposed rocks by temperature changes, frost, plants, animals and human activity — is the key process.

**Factors of soil formation:**
| Factor | Role |
|---|---|
| **Parent rock** | Determines colour, texture, chemical properties, minerals, permeability |
| **Climate** | Temperature and rainfall influence the rate of weathering |
| **Relief** | Altitude and slope decide how soil accumulates |
| **Flora, fauna and micro-organisms** | Affect the rate of humus formation |
| **Time** | Decides the thickness of the soil profile |

**Degradation of soil and conservation.** Soil erosion and depletion are major threats. Human factors — deforestation, overgrazing, overuse of chemical fertilisers or pesticides, rain wash, landslides and floods — degrade soil.

**Methods of soil conservation:**
- **Mulching** — bare ground between plants is covered with organic matter like straw to retain moisture.
- **Contour barriers** — stones, grass and soil build barriers along contours; trenches collect water.
- **Rock dam** — rocks piled to slow the flow of water, preventing gullies.
- **Terrace farming** — broad flat steps on steep slopes so flat surfaces are available to grow crops; reduces surface run-off.
- **Intercropping** — different crops in alternate rows, sown at different times, protect soil from rain wash.
- **Contour ploughing** — ploughing parallel to the contours of a hill slope so furrows form a natural barrier for water.
- **Shelter belts** — rows of trees in coastal and dry regions to check wind movement and protect soil cover.

sections.md:
Fresh water is a vital renewable resource, yet about **three-fourths of the earth is covered with water** while only **2.7%** is fresh water; nearly 70% of that is ice sheets and glaciers in Antarctica, Greenland and mountain regions, so only about **1%** is fit for human use — as groundwater, surface water in rivers and lakes, and water vapour in the atmosphere.

Fresh water can be neither added nor removed; the **water cycle** keeps renewing it. Water is used for drinking, washing, agriculture, industries, generating electricity through reservoirs of dams.

**Problems of water availability.** Shortage in many regions — most of Africa, West Asia, South Asia, parts of western USA, north-west Mexico, parts of South America and the whole of Australia face shortages. Reasons: variation in seasonal or annual rainfall, overexploitation and contamination. Growing population, rising demand for food and cash crops, urbanisation and rising standards of living add to the problem.

**Conservation of water resources:**
- Prevent pollution: treat sewage and industrial effluents before releasing them into water bodies; check run-off of fertilisers and pesticides.
- **Forest and vegetation cover** slows surface run-off and replenishes groundwater.
- **Rainwater harvesting** — collect rainwater on rooftops and store it or recharge groundwater.
- **Canals** used for irrigation should be properly lined to minimise seepage losses.
- **Sprinklers** irrigate effectively, checking losses by seepage and evaporation; **drip or trickle irrigation** is useful in dry regions with high evaporation.
