sections.md:
Some reformers also criticised **caste inequalities**. Rammohun Roy translated an old Buddhist text critical of caste. The **Prarthana Samaj** (western India) adhered to the tradition of **bhakti**, which believed in spiritual equality of all castes. In Bombay, the **Paramhans Mandali** (1840) worked for the abolition of caste; many members were upper-caste and had to hold meetings secretly, sharing food cooked by lower-caste people to break caste rules.

**Missionaries** set up schools for tribal groups and 'lower'-caste children, helping some to gain new skills.

**New work, new hope.** In the nineteenth century, many poor people from lower castes left villages to work in growing cities — in factories, municipalities, as porters, diggers, sweepers or road builders. Some went to plantations in Assam, Mauritius, Trinidad and Indonesia. Work there was hard, but it offered a chance to escape the oppressive grip of upper-caste landowners. The **army** also offered jobs: many Mahars, who were considered 'untouchable', found work in the Mahar Regiment. **B.R. Ambedkar's** father taught at an army school.

**Demands for equality and justice.** From the second half of the nineteenth century, people from non-Brahman castes began organising movements against caste discrimination and demanding social equality and justice.

- The **Satnami movement** in Central India was founded by **Ghasidas**, who worked among leatherworkers and organised a movement to improve their social status.
- In eastern Bengal, **Haridas Thakur's Matua sect** worked among Chandala cultivators, questioning Brahmanical texts that supported caste.
- In present-day Kerala, **Shri Narayana Guru**, from the Ezhava caste, proclaimed the ideal of unity for his people: 'one caste, one religion, one god for humankind'.

All of them founded sects that criticised the caste system.

sections.md:
**Jyotirao Phule (1827–90)**, born into a low-caste family, studied in a Christian missionary school. He developed his own ideas about the injustices of caste society. He attacked the Brahmans' claim that they were superior because they were *Aryans*. Phule argued that the Aryans were outsiders who came from outside the subcontinent and defeated and subjugated the true children of the country — those who had lived there before them. He claimed that before Aryan rule there existed a golden age when warrior-peasants tilled the land and ruled justly.

Phule proposed that the **Shudras** (labouring castes) and **Ati Shudras** ('untouchables') should unite to challenge caste discrimination. The **Satyashodhak Samaj** (1873), founded by Phule, propagated caste equality.

In **1873**, Phule wrote a book named ***Gulamgiri*** (slavery). Some ten years earlier the American Civil War had ended slavery in America. Phule dedicated his book to all those Americans who had fought to free slaves, linking the conditions of 'lower' castes in India and Black slaves in America.

Phule's concern extended to women too. With his wife **Savitribai Phule**, he opened schools for girls. Savitribai is remembered as one of India's first women teachers.

**B.R. Ambedkar (1891–1956)**, born into a Mahar family, experienced caste discrimination in school: he had to sit outside on the ground, and was not allowed to drink water from taps used by upper-caste children. After studying in the USA and England, he returned and wrote extensively against caste. In **1927** he started a **temple entry movement**, in which his Mahar followers participated. Brahman priests were outraged when Dalits used water from a temple tank. Ambedkar led three such movements between 1927 and 1935. His aim was to make everyone see the power of caste prejudices in society.

**E.V. Ramaswamy Naicker (Periyar)** came from a middle-class family. He had been an ascetic and studied Sanskrit scriptures. He became a Congress member but left in disgust when, at a feast organised by nationalists, seating arrangements followed caste distinctions — lower castes made to sit at a distance. Periyar founded the **Self Respect Movement**. He argued that untouchables were the true upholders of an original Tamil and Dravidian culture that had been subjugated by Brahmans. He was an outspoken critic of Hindu scriptures, especially the Codes of Manu, and of texts that he felt established Brahman authority and male control over women.

These assertions did not go unchallenged. Upper-caste nationalist leaders and orthodox groups responded by founding *Sanatan Dharma Sabhas* and the *Bharat Dharma Mahamandal*, arguing for respecting caste as a sacred institution.

check.q: To whom did Jyotirao Phule dedicate Gulamgiri?
options: Americans who fought to free slaves
check.why: Phule dedicated Gulamgiri (1873) to Americans who fought against slavery, linking caste oppression in India with slavery in America.

sections.md:
Reform also came through organisations rooted in religious traditions.

- **Brahmo Samaj** (1830): prohibited all forms of idolatry and sacrifice; believed in the Upanishads; forbade members from criticising other religious practices. It drew on Christianity's ideals too, particularly its messages of love and compassion.
- **Derozio and Young Bengal**: **Henry Louis Vivian Derozio**, a teacher at Hindu College, Calcutta, in the 1820s, encouraged students to question all authority. His students, the 'Young Bengal Movement', attacked tradition, demanded education for women and campaigned for freedom of thought.
- **Ramakrishna Mission**: named after **Ramakrishna Paramhansa**, Swami Vivekananda's guru. The mission stressed the ideal of salvation through social service and selfless action.
- **Prarthana Samaj** (1867, Bombay): sought to remove caste restrictions, abolish child marriage, encourage women's education and end the ban on widow remarriage.
- **Veda Samaj** (1864, Madras): inspired by the Brahmo Samaj; worked to abolish caste distinctions and promote widow remarriage and women's education.
- **Aligarh Movement**: the **Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College**, founded by **Sayyid Ahmed Khan** in **1875** at Aligarh, later became the Aligarh Muslim University. It offered modern education, including Western science, to Muslims.
- **Singh Sabha Movement**: the first Singh Sabhas, reform organisations of the Sikhs, were formed at **Amritsar in 1873** and at **Lahore in 1879**. They sought to rid Sikhism of superstitions, caste distinctions and practices seen as non-Sikh; they promoted education among the Sikhs.

> **Did you know?** The word 'reform' meant different things to different groups. For some it meant returning to an imagined pure past; for others it meant boldly building something new. Both kinds shaped modern India.

rd-school-c9-english-a.ch1-fun-they-had.subtitle: In 2157, a girl finds a paper book and discovers what school used to be

sections.md:
Imagine holding something so strange you can hardly name it: a pile of yellowed sheets, the words printed in one place, refusing to scroll. When you turn back a page, the same words are still sitting there, waiting. For eleven-year-old **Margie**, living in the year **2157**, this is a marvel — a *real book*.

That is the opening idea of **"The Fun They Had"**, a short science-fiction story by **Isaac Asimov**, first published in 1951 (in a newspaper's children's page) and later collected in his book *Earth Is Room Enough* (1957). It is the first chapter of the Class 9 textbook *Beehive*.

The story is tiny — barely a few pages — but it asks a question that feels sharper every year: **what is school actually for?** Is it only for pumping facts into heads efficiently, or is it also about friends, laughter, shared struggle and human teachers?

Asimov wrote this in 1951, long before personal computers, the internet, or online classes. Yet many readers who sat through lockdown-era video lessons in 2020–21 felt the story had been written about them.

> In this read: the author, the setting, a full scene-by-scene retelling, characters, themes, the irony at its heart, language work from the chapter, speaking and writing tasks, and model answers.

Asimov died in 1992, so his story is still under copyright. Read the original in your *Beehive* textbook (free PDF on ncert.nic.in); this companion explains it in its own words without reproducing it.

sections.md:
**Isaac Asimov (1920–1992)** was born in Russia and moved to the United States as a small child, growing up in Brooklyn, New York, where his family ran a sweet shop that also sold magazines — including the pulp science-fiction magazines he devoured. He became a professor of biochemistry at Boston University and one of the most prolific writers who ever lived, writing or editing **around 500 books**.

He is best known for:
- **I, Robot** (1950) and the **Three Laws of Robotics**, which shaped how people imagine robots and AI.
- The **Foundation** series, about a galactic empire's fall and a plan to shorten the dark age that follows.
- Hundreds of popular-science books explaining physics, chemistry, astronomy and history to ordinary readers.

Asimov believed deeply in **learning as joy**. He was largely self-taught in many subjects through libraries. It is no accident that a story by him is about a child who has every fact delivered by machine yet feels something is missing.

**Did you know?** Asimov disliked flying, so despite imagining interstellar travel, he travelled mostly by ship and train in real life.

sections.md:
Asimov builds his future with just a few touches, and each one matters:

- **Telebooks** — books are read on a screen. Margie's family has always had them; paper books are something her grandfather's grandfather remembered being told about.
- **Mechanical teachers** — each child has a robot-like teacher *in their own home*, with a large screen that shows lessons and asks questions.
- **A slot for homework** — children write answers in a **punch code** that they learned at age six, and push the sheets into a slot. The machine calculates marks instantly.
- **Fixed timings** — school happens every day at the same hour, except Saturday and Sunday. Margie's mother believes regular hours help little girls learn better.
- **Lessons adjusted to the child** — the machine is set to each child's ability, so each learns at his or her own pace.

Compare that with today. India already has smart classes, learning apps, AI tutors and auto-graded online tests. Asimov's 2157 is not so far away — which is exactly why the story still bites.

sections.h: The story, retold scene by scene
sections.md:
**Scene 1 — The diary (17 May 2157).** Margie writes in her diary that Tommy has found a real book. She is eleven; her friend **Tommy** is thirteen. He found the book in the attic of his house. Margie's grandfather once said that *his* grandfather had been told, when he was little, that stories were once printed on paper.

**Scene 2 — Reading the book.** The two children turn its crinkly, yellow pages with fascination. They find it funny that the words stay still instead of moving across a screen, and that you could read the same words again just by turning back. Tommy thinks books are wasteful: once you finish, you just throw them away. Their telebook screens can hold a million books and have plenty of room for more.

**Scene 3 — 'School? What's there to write about school?'** The book is about **school** — the kind of school from centuries ago. Margie is scornful at first. She hates school, now more than ever. Recently her mechanical teacher kept giving her geography tests she did worse and worse on, until her mother sadly shook her head and sent for the **County Inspector**.

**Scene 4 — The Inspector (a flashback).** He was a round little man with a red face and a whole box of tools with dials and wires. He smiled at Margie, gave her an apple, and took the teacher apart. Margie hoped he wouldn't know how to put it back together, but he did, within an hour or so — and there it was again, large and black and ugly, with its big screen and the slot for homework. He explained to her mother that the geography sector had been geared **a little too quick**; he slowed it to an average ten-year level, and assured her that the overall pattern of Margie's progress was satisfactory. He patted Margie's head. Margie was disappointed — she had hoped the teacher would be taken away altogether, as Tommy's once was for nearly a month when its history sector blanked out.

**Scene 5 — 'A man? How could a man be a teacher?'** Back in the present, Tommy explains that the old school was not their kind of school: it was the kind of school they had hundreds and hundreds of years ago. In the old days the teacher was **a man** — a real person — not a machine. Margie is astonished: a man isn't smart enough to know as much as a teacher, she argues. Tommy, loftily, insists the old teacher knew almost as much as his own father. And how could a strange man come into your house to teach you? Tommy laughs: the teacher didn't live in the house. There was a **special building**, and all the kids went there. They **learned the same things** at the same time, if they were the same age.

**Scene 6 — The call to school.** Margie wants to read more, but her mother calls: it is time for school. Tommy says he will come back later — maybe. Margie reluctantly goes to the schoolroom, right next to her bedroom. The mechanical teacher is on and waiting; it is always on at the same time every day except weekends. Today it is arithmetic — adding **proper fractions**. The screen lights up and the teacher speaks about today's lesson. Margie sighs and inserts yesterday's homework into the slot.

**Scene 7 — The daydream.** While the machine drones on, Margie thinks about the old schools: kids from the whole neighbourhood coming together, laughing and shouting in the schoolyard, sitting together in the schoolroom, going home together at the end of the day. They learned the same things, so they could help one another with homework and talk about it. And the teachers were people.

**Ending.** The mechanical teacher flashes a question about fractions. Margie is still thinking about how the children of the old days must have loved it, and about **the fun they had**.

sections.md:
**Margie Jones** (11) — the heart of the story. Bright but bored and lonely; she *hates school* because it is mechanical, solitary and relentless. She is imaginative: by the end she is daydreaming about schoolyards and friends. Her feelings change from **scorn** to **longing**.

**Tommy** (13) — confident, a little superior, likes to show off his knowledge. He scoffs at books as wasteful but knows more about the old schools, and he enjoys teaching Margie. His swaggering 'Sure' and the narrator's word *loftily* reveal a typical older-kid tone.

**Margie's mother** — practical, believes in routine. Insists that little girls learn better with regular hours. She represents adults who trust the system.

**The County Inspector** — round, red-faced, cheerful, with a box full of tools. He fixes the machine efficiently and reassures Margie's mother that the fault isn't the child's. He is kind, but his solution is technical; nobody asks whether Margie is *happy*.

**The mechanical teacher** — not a character with feelings, but a powerful presence: large, black and ugly in Margie's eyes, with a big screen, a slot, endless tests. It treats every child as an input-output problem.

sections.h: Themes: what is the story really about?
sections.md:
**1. Human connection in learning.** The machine teaches efficiently, but Margie is miserable. What she imagines missing is not *information* but *people*: classmates, a schoolyard, a human teacher who laughs and explains.

**2. Technology vs. humanity.** Asimov loved technology, yet he shows its limits. The telebook holds a million books; the paper book holds a story Margie can touch. The Inspector can fix the gear-speed of geography, but not loneliness.

**3. Nostalgia and the grass-is-greener effect.** Margie romanticises old schools. Real old-time schools had strict teachers, rote learning, bullying, even canes. Asimov hints at this gently: children of the past often complained about school too! The story invites us to see that **every generation idealises the past**.

**4. Standardisation vs. personalisation.** In 2157 each child learns at their own pace — something modern educators actually want. In the past, all children learned 'the same things'. Margie thinks the old way sounds wonderful because it is *shared*. There is a real trade-off here.

**5. The value of the physical book.** The book is permanent, tactile and shared — Tommy and Margie read it together, heads bent over the same page.

**Discussion for you:** During online classes, what did you miss most — the content, or the people? Your answer is the story's argument.

sections.md:
**Irony** is when there is a gap between what is expected and what happens. This story is full of it:

- **Dramatic irony:** We, the readers, *are* the children of the 'old schools'. We know school isn't always fun — yet Margie imagines it was paradise. Our grumbles about school become her dream.
- **Situational irony:** Tommy calls the book a waste of paper, yet it is the book that opens the most exciting idea the children have had.
- **The title itself** — *The Fun They Had* — is gently ironic. Was it really fun? From Margie's lonely seat, yes.

**Craft features:**
- **Diary opening** — the story starts with Margie's diary entry, pulling us into the future with a single date.
- **Economy** — Asimov uses very few words; the future is sketched through everyday details (telebooks, punch code, a slot), not long explanations.
- **Dialogue** reveals character: Tommy's boastful replies and Margie's indignant questions.
- **Flashback** — the Inspector's visit is told in the middle, explaining why Margie hates school.
- **Open ending** — we are left inside Margie's daydream, with the mechanical teacher droning on about fractions.

sections.h: Beyond the story: did Asimov predict the future?
sections.md:
Read the story again with a 2020s eye and tick off what has come true:

| Asimov's 2157 | Our world today |
|---|---|
| Telebooks holding a million books | E-readers, PDFs, NCERT e-pathshala, digital libraries |
| Mechanical teacher at home | Learning apps, video lessons, AI tutors |
| Homework marked instantly | Auto-graded online quizzes and OMR sheets |
| Lessons geared to each child's level | 'Adaptive' learning software |
| County Inspector repairing the machine | Tech support, software updates |
| Children learning alone | Lockdown-era online schooling, 2020–21 |

What has **not** happened (yet)? Schools have not disappeared. After the pandemic, most families and teachers were eager to get children back into classrooms — which is almost exactly Margie's conclusion. Researchers found that children missed friends, play and the encouragement of a teacher who notices when they are sad.

**The balanced view.** Technology is good at speed, practice and personal pace. Humans are good at care, motivation, discussion, values and fun. The best schools today try to blend both. Asimov's story is not anti-technology; it is a warning against using technology to remove the *human* part of learning.

**Did you know?** In 1951, when the story was written, a single computer filled an entire room and very few people had ever seen one. Asimov imagined home teaching screens decades before personal computers existed.

check.q: Which statement best captures the story's view of technology?
options: Technology is evil and should be banned
Technology is useful, but learning also needs human company
Machines are better teachers than humans
check.why: The story shows the machine as efficient but lonely; its point is that learning needs a human side, not that technology is bad.

sections.h: Thinking about language: adverbs and more
sections.md:
**1. Adverbs of manner.** Asimov uses adverbs to show *how* characters speak and act — 'Tommy said loftily', 'Margie said scornfully', 'her mother shook her head sorrowfully', 'Tommy said nonchalantly'. Adverbs of this kind are often formed by adding **-ly** to an adjective, with spelling changes:

| Adjective | Adverb | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| angry | angrily | y → i + ly |
| happy | happily | y → i + ly |
| easy | easily | y → i + ly |
| sorrowful | sorrowfully | + ly |
| scornful | scornfully | + ly |
| careful | carefully | + ly |
| nonchalant | nonchalantly | + ly |
| loud | loudly | + ly |
| terrible | terribly | -le → -ly |
| gentle | gently | -le → -ly |

Try it: rewrite 'Margie went to the schoolroom' with *reluctantly*, then with *eagerly*. Notice how one word changes the character's mood.

**2. Adverbs of time, place and degree.** The story also uses words like *once*, *then*, *right next to*, *awfully*, *nearly*. 'Awfully funny' in the story is informal and means *very strange*, not 'terrible'.

**3. The past perfect for earlier events.** When Margie remembers the Inspector's visit, we move to an even earlier past: 'The Inspector *had* smiled… he *had* taken the teacher apart.' Use **had + past participle** for the earlier of two past actions. Example: *By the time Margie reached the schoolroom, the teacher had already switched on.*

**4. Reported speech.**
- Direct: Tommy said, "I found a real book."
- Reported: Tommy said that he had found a real book.
- Direct: Margie asked, "What's there to write about school?"
- Reported: Margie asked what there was to write about school.

**5. Useful words**

| Word / phrase | Meaning in context |
|---|---|
| crinkly | full of small creases (old paper pages) |
| scornful | showing contempt |
| loftily | in a superior, proud way |
| dispute | argue about |
| sector | a part (of the machine) for one subject |
| geared | adjusted to suit |
| nonchalantly | casually, without concern |
| sorrowfully | sadly |

sections.md:
**Speaking — class debate.** Topic: *'Home schooling with a machine is better than going to school.'* Prepare three points for each side.
- For: own pace, no travel, instant feedback, can repeat lessons.
- Against: loneliness, no friends or play, no teacher to notice feelings, screen strain, less teamwork.
Use phrases: 'I'd like to begin by…', 'On the other hand…', 'I respectfully disagree because…', 'To sum up…'.

**Writing — a paragraph or letter.** *Where would you prefer to study — at home with a machine, or at school with other children? Why?* Plan:
1. Opening sentence with your choice.
2. Two or three reasons with examples from your own life (a group project, a teacher who helped you, a cricket match at recess).
3. One line acknowledging the other side.
4. Closing sentence.

**Creative — Margie's next diary entry.** Write 100 words in Margie's voice for 18 May 2157. Include one future detail (perhaps the teacher breaks again!) and one feeling about the old book.

**Dictionary skill.** Look up *punch*, *gear* and *sector* in a dictionary. Each has several meanings — find the one that fits the story.

**Q1. What kind of book did Tommy find?** *(30–40 words)*
**Model:** Tommy found a real, old paper book in the attic of his house. Its pages were yellow and crinkly, and its words stayed still. It was about school as it was hundreds of years earlier.

**Q2. Why did Margie hate school?** *(30–40 words)*
**Model:** Margie hated school because she studied alone with a mechanical teacher at home. It gave her test after test, especially in geography, which had been set too fast for her. There were no classmates or human teacher.

**Q3. What had once happened to Tommy's teacher?** *(30 words)*
**Model:** Tommy's mechanical teacher had once been taken away for nearly a month because its history sector had blanked out completely. Margie wished the same would happen to hers.

**Q4. How did Margie's mother and the Inspector handle her poor geography marks?** *(40 words)*
**Model:** Her mother sent for the County Inspector. He took the machine apart, found the geography sector was geared too quickly, slowed it to an average ten-year level and assured her mother that Margie's overall progress was satisfactory.

**Q5. What did Margie think about the old schools, and why did she think the children loved it?** *(100–120 words)*
**Model outline:** Start with what Tommy told her: a real man was the teacher, and children of the same age learned together in a special building. Then explain Margie's imagination: children laughing and shouting in the schoolyard, sitting together, going home together, helping each other with homework. Link to her own experience: her mechanical teacher was relentless and solitary. Conclude: she felt the old-time children must have loved school because it was social and human — the 'fun they had'. Add one line of your own view (e.g. modern blended learning tries to combine both).

**Q6. Do you agree that schools today are more fun than the school of the future described in the story?** *(100–120 words)* — give your view, two reasons with examples, and acknowledge one benefit of machine learning.

**Tips:**
1. Name the character and the detail ('the County Inspector slowed the geography sector').
2. Use your own sentences; never copy long lines from the text.
3. For long answers: introduction → 2–3 points with evidence → conclusion with your view.
